In brief

Two elements of traditional fairy tales float through Gerty's mind in the passage where her dreams shift from Reggy Wylie to an older mate. Imagining herself in front of the mirror in her bedroom, she imagines it saying, "You are lovely, Gerty"—clearly a reference to the magic mirror of "Snow White." Later in the same paragraph, giving up on Reggy, she thinks, "No prince charming is her beau ideal to lay a rare and wondrous love at her feet." Prince Charming is a generic popular name for the male type that recurs in fairy tales like "Snow White," "Sleeping Beauty," "Rapunzel," and "Cinderella." These staples of Gerty's imagination suggest that she may have held on to childhood fictions a bit too long. Joyce confirms the impression by dropping a hilarious age-specific detail into the narrative.

At more length

"Snow White," first published in the Grimm brothers' collection in 1812 and revised in their final 1857 edition, tells the story of a young princess who is murderously envied by her stepmother. The evil queen possesses a magic mirror, and every morning she asks it, "Mirror, mirror, on the wall, who's the fairest of them all?" The mirror always answers "You are," until the day when the queen's beauty is outstripped by seven-year-old Snow White's. Thus begins a series of harrowing adventures that ends in the woodland cottage of some dwarves when a poisoned apple appears to take the young girl's life. A young prince shows up at the cottage, falls in love with the dead girl, and offers to take her corpse back to her father's castle. On the trip there, a jolt dislodges the apple from her throat, she wakes up, the prince proposes, and she accepts.

All of this bears some loose connection to Gerty, who has spent years waiting for Reggy Wylie to grow up and propose marriage to her. The thought of spinsterhood brings tears to her eyes "and she would give worlds to be in the privacy of her own familiar chamber where, giving way to tears, she could have a good cry and relieve her pentup feelings. Though not too much because she knew how to cry nicely before the mirror. You are lovely, Gerty, it said." Gerty is fairest of all the girls in her neck of the woods, and remaining constantly beautiful is her one hope of reaching the happy ending that her life deserves. But what an ordeal, the endless waiting!

The "prince charming" of such stories (though often not known by that name—it may have entered the English lexicon via Andrew Lang's The Blue Fairy Book in 1889) exists to reward a plucky, good-hearted, and very pretty girl with marriage into a prominent and wealthy family. That too has obvious relevance to Gerty's life, since the Wylies are well-off Protestants and Reggie, she assumes, will be "going to Trinity college to study for a doctor" after he graduates from high school. When he does the right thing by her he will "lay a rare and wondrous love at her feet" and she will be, not an unimportant neighborhood girl, but Mrs. Gertrude Wylie, "wearing a sumptuous confection of grey trimmed with expensive blue fox."

These evocations of fairy tales are not so much literary allusions as cultural archetypes—commonly accepted roles for a dreamy girl to imagine playing in the process of growing up—and Joyce slyly insinuates that growing up is something that Gerty MacDowell has yet to do. Not only is she young, but she is fixated on a boy who is much younger (perhaps 17), and her obsession with him began when he was younger still: "He was too young to understand. He would not believe in love, a woman's birthright. The night of the party long ago in Stoers' (he was still in short trousers) when they were alone and he stole an arm round her waist she went white to the very lips. He called her little one in a strangely husky voice and snatched a half kiss (the first!) but it was only the end of her nose and then he hastened from the room with a remark about refreshments." This sounds like an account of a college freshman trying out his moves, as does her reaction: "Impetuous fellow! Strength of character had never been Reggy Wylie's strong point and he who would woo and win Gerty MacDowell must be a man among men." But manhood is a ludicrously inappropriate concept.

The party happened "long ago," and the detail of "short trousers" suggests that Reggy was barely (if precociously) pubescent. Citing Laura Ugolini's Men and Meanswear (2007), Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner note that "While there would have been certain differences between the social classes, in general it would be expected that boys would wear only short trousers until around the age of 12 or 13, at which point they would transition to long trousers." Far from being a man among men, Prince Charming Reggy, Lady-killer Reggy, was not even a teenager among teenagers. The realization that Gerty has, for years, been dreaming about marrying someone who kissed her when he was scarcely ten years out of nappies makes clear that she too is a bit "too young to understand."

John Hunt 2026
